adopt.found.name: ● {name}
adopt.found.notooling: Nothing to replace: it has no lint, test or build tool of its own.
adopt.found.blockers: {blockers} to clear before smith can go on:
adopt.found.install: Nothing has changed yet. Installing only fills node_modules, which git does not track, so git cannot take it back. None of your own files are touched.
adopt.found.root: The project ({manifest}, {name}) is at the repository root. smith manages one folder per project, so the next screen asks where to move it. smith does not choose the folder for you.
adopt.found.unchanged.root: Nothing has changed. The screens after list every file before anything is written.
adopt.found.unchanged: Nothing has changed. The next screens ask how far to go and list every file before anything is written.
adopt.convert.title: ● Convert the {source} {name} to smith, keeping what works
adopt.convert.body:
smith takes over from {tool}. It adds its settings file (smith.toml), turns each {tool} task into a task
  smith runs, removes {tool} and the files only it used, and replaces the CI pipeline files with ones
  it generates (your own steps go in the marked sections). Your code is not rewritten. How each
  project lints, tests and builds is carried over where smith can; what behaves differently or needs
  you is listed below. Every change is a file in git, so git can take it back.
adopt.writes.moved: Writes smith.toml and the CI pipelines for the project once it is moved (or an empty workspace if it stays);
adopt.writes.found: Writes smith.toml and the CI pipelines for the {count} projects found;
adopt.writes.kept: your build and lint setup stay as they are. smith doctor then says what is left to do.
adopt.commit.box: {box} Commit this change so it can be undone (press c to tick it)
adopt.review.header: ● Nothing has changed yet. The files below are what the conversion writes. After it, smith asks about each group of old files before deleting anything. Every change is a file in git, so git can take it back.
adopt.group.empty.keys: y changes them · n keeps them as they are · s keeps these and skips the groups after
adopt.group.delete: ● We are going to delete {counts}. {reason} — ok?
adopt.group.keys: y deletes them · n keeps them · s keeps these and skips the groups after
adopt.done.empty: ● {name} has a smith.toml now, but smith found no project in it
adopt.done.empty.hint: Add one with smith add, or move your code into folders that hold a manifest (package.json, go.mod, pyproject.toml).
adopt.done.declined: Left as they were, as you chose: {list}
adopt.done.committed: Committed as one change: smith undo reverts it.
adopt.done.uncommitted: Not committed: review with git status. git can take the changes back.
adopt.done.findings: ▲ Found by the closing checks ({count}): the conversion finished, these need you
adopt.done.changed.more: • and {count} more: the full list is in {file}
adopt.done.kept: Looks like the old tooling but stays (something still uses it):
adopt.done.open: Enter opens the workspace. The full report is saved in {file}; press s to read it here.
adopt.done.open.first: Open the workspace to see it, or let smith build everything first to check that it works.
adopt.init.desc: smith will write smith.toml and the pipelines. These choices change files of yours, so smith asks. The first answer of each changes the least; the next screen shows every file with a diff before anything is written.
adopt.init.ask: how smith sets up the repository
adopt.move.other: another folder: {name} (edit the text; it is the whole folder, such as tools/web)
adopt.move.none: : smith adopts an empty workspace and the project stays at the root
adopt.split.desc: Moving the project also splits what belongs to the workspace from what belongs to the project. smith moves the tools to the workspace on its own. It asks about what it cannot place. The first answer of each changes the least.
adopt.split.dep.question: {name} is a development dependency, and smith does not know it as a tool. Where should it go?
adopt.split.dep.project: The project: it stays in the project's own manifest
adopt.split.dep.workspace: The workspace: it moves to the workspace's manifest, for every project
adopt.split.lint.question: The project has its own ESLint setup. What should happen to it?
adopt.split.lint.keep: Keep my own ESLint setup in the project
adopt.split.lint.shared: Use the shared config: the old file is kept as .pre-smith and the ESLint packages leave the project
adopt.summary.files: Files: smith creates {created}, edits {edited} and removes {removed}.
adopt.summary.checkhead: ! Check these before you go ahead ({count})
adopt.summary.more: • and {count} more: the full list is saved in {file} once it is converted
adopt.reading.headline: Reading the repository…
adopt.cancel.stopped: Stopped. The conversion is in your files; git status shows it, and git restore --staged --worktree . && git clean -fd takes it back (installed packages stay installed).
adopt.cancel.closed: Closed. Whatever ran is in your files; git status shows it and git can take it back (installed packages stay installed).
adopt.error.again: could not read the repository again
adopt.style.name: Bring in
adopt.level.question: How far should smith go?
adopt.level.conservative: Conservative: keep what works, map what can be mapped and list the rest as things to check
adopt.level.full: Full: make smith the only tool, replacing the old lint, test, build and CI tooling and deleting what is left over, asking about each group first
adopt.choices.desc: Full level: smith becomes the only tool. The first option of each question is the one this repository's own tooling suggests.
adopt.job.prepare: working out what the conversion leaves behind

adopt.plan.headline: Planning what the choices remove…

The MonoSmith agent lets Claude Code and VS Code work in this workspace through smith.
It reads on its own and asks before it changes anything.
